newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GOVT REJECTS CHANGING CURRENCY, TRADE POLICY.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GOVT REJECTS CHANGING CURRENCY, TRADE POLICY.

text.p: The Czech government approved a paper on export policy, rejecting demands that changes in tariff and exchange rate policy were needed to stem the growing trade deficit, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Wednesday.
"The government does not intend to do major changes in pro-export policy, anti-import policy, and no changes in exchange rate or import-surcharge policy," Klaus said after a cabinet session.
The paper was not yet available.

Government and central bank officials have repeatedly ruled out a devalutaion of the Czech crown as a way boost exports and close a trade deficit which has forced forecasts of the 1996 current account deficit to grow to more than seven percent of gross domestic product from four percent in 1995.
Some analysts and exporters have called for a devaluation of the Czech currency or other protectionist measures to help balance growing trade problems.

At the end of the last year, the lower house of the Czech parliament, the Chamber of Deputies, in which the centre-right government is in a minority, requested the government to prepare an export support plan.

The trade deficit reached 140.1 billion crowns in the first 11 months of 1996, and is expected to hit a record high of about 160 billion for the whole of the year after a 96 billion crown deficit in 1995.
The Czech Statistical Burau has forecast the deficit to reach 211 to 219 billion crowns this year.

Klaus said that the cabinet agreed to make no major changes, and would look toward possible readjustment of taxation and write-off rules, and promote financial restructuring of some companies or sectors.
He did not give more details on these proposals.
